claim: Axolotls and other salamanders can regenerate entire limbs after amputation as adults.
source: Axolotls and other salamanders can regenerate entire limbs after amputation as adults, and much recent effort has sought to identify the molecular programs controlling this process.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of regenerative biology, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The regenerated limb is a high-fidelity replicate of the original limb in mosaic mutant axolotls.
source: Previously, we quantified CRISPR/Cas9-generated mutations in the limbs of mosaic mutant axolotls before and after regeneration and found that the regenerated limb is a highfidelity replicate of the original limb (Flowers et al. 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Flowers et al. 2017).

claim: Salamanders are the only vertebrates known to regenerate complete limbs as adults.
source: Salamanders are the only vertebrates known to regenerate complete limbs as adults.
evidence: This represents established scientific knowledge in the field of regenerative biology.

claim: The axolotl can regenerate limbs, tails, and gills without scarring.
source: The axolotl, a species of salamander, can regenerate limbs, tails, and gills without scarring.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axolotl regenerative capabilities.

claim: Regeneration of complex structures occurs through the formation of a blastema.
source: Regeneration of these complex structures occurs through the formation of a blastema, a mass of proliferating dedifferentiated cells and pre-existing progenitor and stem cells (Currie et al., 2016; Kragl et al., 2009; Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A blastema is a mass of proliferating dedifferentiated cells and pre-existing progenitor and stem cells.
source: Regeneration of these complex structures occurs through the formation of a blastema, a mass of proliferating dedifferentiated cells and pre-existing progenitor and stem cells (Currie et al., 2016; Kragl et al., 2009; Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Transcriptional profiling of the limb blastema has produced long lists of candidate genes that remain largely uncharacterized.
source: Transcriptional profiling of the limb blastema has produced long lists of candidate genes that, to date, remain largely uncharacterized (Bryant et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2011; Gerber et al., 2018; Knapp et al., 2013; Leigh et al., 2018; Monaghan et al., 2009; Voss et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to transcriptional profiling studies.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has made the axolotl a genetically tractable organism.
source: The advent of CRISPR/Cas9 has made the axolotl a genetically tractable organism and the functional interrogation of these genes possible (Flowers et al., 2014; Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating CRISPR/Cas9 application in axolotls.

claim: Near-complete knockout F0 axolotl animals appear to be universally mosaic, harboring a variety of mutant alleles.
source: Although near-complete knockout F0 animals can be generated, they appear to be universally mosaic, harboring a variety of mutant alleles (Flowers et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Embryonically generated mutations both perturb gene function and uniquely label affected cell lineages with a traceable genetic barcode.
source: Such embryonically generated mutations both perturb the function of the targeted gene and uniquely label affected cell lineages with a traceable genetic barcode.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of CRISPR-generated mutations in mosaic animals.

claim: The majority of very low-frequency alleles reoccur in a regenerated limb at a frequency strikingly similar to that of the original limb.
source: We found that the majority of very low-frequency alleles reoccur in a regenerated limb at a frequency strikingly similar to that of the original limb.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the authors' previous study using NGS to quantify mutant allele frequencies.

claim: Limb regeneration is a high-fidelity process in which the contributions of small cell populations to the original limb are replicated in the regenerated limb.
source: These data indicate that limb regeneration is a high-fidelity process in which the contributions of small cell populations to the original limb are replicated in the regenerated limb (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' previous work and illustrated in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Cell identities converge at a transcriptional level during regeneration in the axolotl limb blastema.
source: Recent single-cell sequencing of the axolotl limb blastema demonstrated that cell identities converge at a transcriptional level during regeneration (Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a single-cell sequencing study.

claim: Transcriptional convergence suggests a shared genetic program across most blastemal cells.
source: This suggests a shared genetic program across most blastemal cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of transcriptional convergence.

claim: Genetic perturbation of critical blastema-enriched genes would impair mutagenized cells' ability to participate in the regenerative process.
source: We anticipated that genetic perturbation of critical blastema-enriched genes would impair mutagenized cells' ability to participate in the regenerative process.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the shared genetic program across blastemal cells.

claim: Negative selection screens are widely used to identify genes essential for cellular processes with CRISPR/Cas.
source: Negative selection screens are widely used to identify genes essential for cellular processes with CRISPR/Cas (Shalem et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Yin and Chen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on CRISPR screening methods.

claim: Screening can be improved by using haploid cells, which harbor a single copy of each gene and require monoallelic inactivation to unveil loss-of-function phenotypes.
source: Screening can be improved by using haploid cells, which harbor a single copy of each gene, and thus require monoallelic inactivation to unveil loss-of-function phenotypes.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the advantages of haploid genetic screens.

claim: Gynogenetic haploids were generated through in vitro activation of eggs using UV-enucleated sperm.
source: We generated gynogenetic haploids through in vitro activation of eggs from white or transgenic RFP+ females using UV-enucleated sperm from a transgenic GFP+ male (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Haploidy was confirmed by karyotype analysis showing n = 14 chromosomes in 3/3 embryos.
source: Haploidy was confirmed by karyotype (n = 14, 3/3 embryos, three squashes/embryo, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from karyotype analysis.

claim: Haploidy was confirmed by the universal appearance of the haploid syndrome embryonic phenotype in 120/120 embryos.
source: the universal appearance of the haploid syndrome embryonic phenotype (120/120 embryos, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C; Hronowski et al., 1979)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to prior work describing the haploid syndrome.

claim: Haploidy was confirmed by complete absence of paternally-derived GFP expression in 156/156 donor embryos.
source: complete absence of paternally-derived GFP expression in donor embryos (156/156 GFP-, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing absence of GFP expression.

claim: Adult haploid axolotls are not viable.
source: Adult haploid axolotls are not viable, so we developed reliable whole limb bud grafting techniques to generate chimeric axolotls with haploid limbs (Figure 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about haploid axolotl viability.

claim: Embryos grafted at stage 23–25 produced normally developed limbs with a consistent host-derived neural GFP+ expression pattern.
source: Embryos grafted at stage 23–25 produced normally developed limbs with a consistent host-derived neural GFP+ expression pattern (Figure 2B; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from grafting experiments.

claim: Cleanly grafted haploid limbs develop fully, but are smaller and shorter than the opposing diploid limbs of the same animals.
source: We found that cleanly grafted haploid limbs develop fully, but are smaller and shorter than the opposing diploid limbs of the same animals (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and images.

claim: Haploid-diploid chimeras exhibited a neural-GFP expression pattern similar to diploid-diploid chimeras.
source: Furthermore, haploid-diploid chimeras (HDCs) exhibited a neural-GFP expression pattern similar to DDCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Both HDC and DDC graft limbs fully regenerate and retain their neural GFP expression pattern.
source: We amputated HDC and DDC limbs and found that both fully regenerate and retain their neural GFP expression pattern (2/2 HDC limbs, 2/2 DDC limbs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from amputation and regeneration experiments.

claim: Haploid limb regeneration is slightly delayed relative to diploid limb regeneration.
source: While the gross morphology of regenerated haploid limbs is identical to that of the original limbs, haploid limb regeneration is slightly delayed relative to diploid limb regeneration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: NGS of targeted loci in 12 HDCs revealed 92 total alleles with a mean mutation frequency of 3.46% per allele in the primary limbs.
source: NGS of targeted loci in 12 HDCs mutagenized with one of two highly active guide RNAs (gRNAs) revealed 92 total alleles with a mean mutation frequency of 3.46% per allele in the primary limbs (SE = + /- 1.19%).
evidence: This claim is supported by NGS data from the study.

claim: The log score of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the primary limbs predicts the log score of the normalized read numbers in the secondary limbs (R2 = 0.544, p<0.0001).
source: NGS of these targeted sites in DNA from regenerated limbs revealed that the log score of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the primary limbs predicts the log score of the normalized read numbers in the secondary limbs (R2 = 0.544, p<0.0001, Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of NGS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: With respect to morphology and cell lineage contributions, haploid limb regeneration is similar to that of diploid limb regeneration.
source: Thus, with respect to morphology and cell lineage contributions, haploid limb regeneration is similar to that of diploid limb regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on allele frequencies and morphology.

claim: 76.1% (70/92) of tyrosinase and methyltransferase-like alleles are detected in both the first and second haploid limbs.
source: The majority of tyrosinase and methyltransferase-like alleles (76.1%, 70/92) are detected in both the first and second haploid limbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of allele detection data.

claim: 81.5% (75/92) of mutant alleles occur at a low frequency, comprising fewer than 1.6% of the total reads for a given haploid limb.
source: Most mutant alleles occur at a low frequency, comprising fewer than 1.6% of the total reads for a given haploid limb (81.5%, 75/92, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of allele frequency data shown in Table 1.

claim: 70.7% (53/75) of low-frequency alleles are detected in both primary and secondary limbs.
source: The majority of low-frequency alleles are detected in both primary and secondary limbs (70.7%, 53/75)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of allele detection data.

claim: 69.3% (52/75) of low-frequency alleles undergo less than a two-fold change in frequency after regeneration.
source: undergo less than a two-fold change in frequency after regeneration (69.3%, 52/75, Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of allele frequency changes shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Haploid limb regeneration is a high-fidelity process in which the majority of small cell lineages contribute to the regenerated limb in a manner similar to their contributions to the original developed limb.
source: Collectively, these results support the notion that, as in diploids, haploid limb regeneration is a high-fidelity process in which the majority of small cell lineages contribute to the regenerated limb in a manner similar to their contributions to the original developed limb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the collective experimental data on allele frequencies.

claim: Fetuin-b and catalase exhibited signs of negative selection, showing both a loss of mutant alleles and a decline in the contribution of mutant alleles from primary to secondary limbs.
source: We found two genes, fetuin-b and catalase, that exhibited signs of negative selection, showing both a loss of mutant alleles and a decline in the contribution of mutant alleles from primary to secondary limbs (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of allele frequency data shown in Table 1.

claim: The slope of the linear regression of fetuin-b alleles (m = 0.254) is significantly different from controls (m = 0.861, p<0.0001).
source: We compared the linear regression line slopes of all mutant alleles between primary and secondary limbs for each target gene with those of the inessential controls (methyltransferase-like and tyrosinase) and found that fetuin-b (fetub) was significantly different (n = 48 mutant alleles, fetub m = 0.254, controls m = 0.861, p<0.0001, Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANCOVA) of allele frequency data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The slope of the linear regression of fetuin-b (m = 0.254) is lower than that of all other target genes combined (m = 0.619, p=0.009).
source: Further comparison of fetub with all other target genes combined reveals that the slope of the linear regression of fetub is lower than that of all other target genes combined (fetub m = 0.254, All other target genes m = 0.619, p=0.009, ANCOVA, Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANCOVA) shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Linear regression analysis of fetuin-b reveals that the log scores of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the second limb poorly predict the log scores in the primary limb (R2 = 0.069, p=0.046).
source: Linear regression analysis of fetub reveals that the log scores of the normalized read numbers for each allele in the second limb poorly predict the log scores of the normalized read numbers in the primary limb (R2 = 0.069, p=0.046, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Fetuin-b alleles detected in the primary limb are more likely to be absent in the secondary limb (45.8%, 22/48) than alleles detected in controls (23.9%, 22/92), and this difference is significant (χ2 = 7.03, p=0.008).
source: Alleles of fetub detected in the primary limb are more likely to be absent in the secondary limb (45.8%, 22/48) than alleles detected in controls (23.9%, 22/92) and this difference is significant (χ2 = 7.03, p=0.008).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) of allele loss data.

claim: The slope of the linear regression of catalase alleles (m = 0.018) differed from control genes (m = 0.861, p=0.005).
source: Similarly, the slope of the linear regression of catalase alleles differed from control genes (n = 8 mutant alleles, catalase m = 0.018, controls m = 0.861, p=0.005, ANCOVA, Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANCOVA) shown in Figure 5.

claim: The slope of the linear regression of catalase (m = 0.018) differed from all other target genes excluding fetuin-b (m = 0.645, p=0.029).
source: The slope of the linear regression of catalase did not differ from that of all other target genes combined, except when fetub was excluded (catalase m = 0.018, all other target genes m = 0.550, p=0.073, all other target genes excluding fetub m = 0.645, p=0.029, ANCOVA, Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANCOVA) shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significantly greater proportion of catalase alleles are lost (75.5%, 6/8) than both those of controls and all other targets combined (χ2 = 9.53, p=0.002 and χ2 = 5.81, p=0.016, respectively).
source: A significantly greater proportion of catalase alleles are lost (75.5%, 6/8) than both those of controls and all other targets combined (χ2 = 9.53, p=0.002 and χ2 = 5.81, p=0.016, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) of allele loss data.

claim: Early embryonic mutants for catalase and fetuin-b were confirmed to have high-level mutagenesis by fluorescent PCR fragment analysis.
source: We extracted DNA from the amputated tails and confirmed the high-level mutagenesis of fetub and catalase by fluorescent PCR fragment analysis (fetub, n = 12, mean = 7.3% wildtype alleles, SD = + /- 5.2%;. catalase, n = 16, mean = 3.0% wildtype alleles, SD = + /- 5.8%, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR fragment analysis data.

claim: Fetuin-b and catalase mutants did not display regeneration growth defects compared to tyrosinase mutants at early time points.
source: fetub and catalase mutants did not display regeneration growth defects compared to tyrosinase mutants at early time points
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of tail regeneration.

claim: The total regenerative outgrowth of both fetuin-b and catalase mutant tails were reduced compared to tyrosinase mutants at 18 days post-amputation (p=0.002 for fetuin-b; p=0.012 for catalase).
source: but the total regenerative outgrowth of both fetub and catalase mutant tails were reduced compared to tyrosinase mutants at 18 days post-amputation (n = 16 tyrosinase mutants, p=0.002, fetub; p=0.012, catalase; Welch's t-test, one-tailed; Figure 6A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of tail regeneration measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reduction in regeneration was also evident at 14 days post-amputation in catalase mutant tails (p=0.025).
source: with the reduction in regeneration also evident at 14 days post-amputation in catalase mutant tails (p=0. 025, Welch's t-test, one-tailed, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of tail regeneration measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: While catalase and fetuin-b are not essential for the onset of regeneration, the process of regeneration is slower in the tails of catalase and fetuin-b mutants.
source: These data indicate that, while catalase and fetub are not essential for the onset of regeneration, the process of regeneration is slower in the tails of catalase and fetub mutants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tail regeneration data showing delayed but not absent regeneration.

claim: The findings are consistent with the apparent loss of catalase and fetuin-b mutant cells within the context of regenerating mosaic mutant haploid limbs.
source: These findings are consistent with the apparent loss of catalase and fetub mutant cells within the context of regenerating mosaic mutant haploid limbs and suggest a broader role for these genes in the regeneration of multiple tissues and structures.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the tail regeneration data to the limb regeneration data.

claim: Catalase and fetuin-b have a broader role in the regeneration of multiple tissues and structures.
source: These findings are consistent with the apparent loss of catalase and fetub mutant cells within the context of regenerating mosaic mutant haploid limbs and suggest a broader role for these genes in the regeneration of multiple tissues and structures.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that both limb and tail regeneration are affected.

claim: Cell competition in developing tissues can result in the elimination of cells lacking genes controlling the rate of growth at a whole organismal level.
source: As cell competition in developing tissues can result in the elimination of cells lacking genes controlling the rate of growth at a whole organismal level (Johnston et al., 1999; Morata and Ripoll, 1975), these findings support the validity of this assay as a means to identify genes critical for proper regeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cell competition.

claim: The findings support the validity of this assay as a means to identify genes critical for proper regeneration.
source: As cell competition in developing tissues can result in the elimination of cells lacking genes controlling the rate of growth at a whole organismal level (Johnston et al., 1999; Morata and Ripoll, 1975), these findings support the validity of this assay as a means to identify genes critical for proper regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the successful identification of catalase and fetuin-b.

claim: Catalase is an enzyme that plays a conserved role in protecting cells from oxidative damage by catalyzing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.
source: Catalase is an enzyme that plays a conserved role in protecting cells from oxidative damage by catalyzing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, a reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about catalase function.

claim: ROS are critical for normal tail, fin, and heart regeneration to proceed in xenopus and zebrafish.
source: Despite their potentially harmful effects, ROS are critical for normal tail, fin, and heart regeneration to proceed in xenopus and zebrafish (Love et al., 2013; Gauron et al., 2013; Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on ROS in regeneration.

claim: Prolonged ROS-exposure and ROS-induced cellular senescence impair tissue regeneration.
source: However, prolonged ROS-exposure and ROS-induced cellular senescence impair tissue regeneration (Saxena et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of catalase impedes heart regeneration after infarction in zebrafish.
source: Overexpression of catalase impedes heart regeneration after infarction in zebrafish, and chemical inhibition of Catalase may transiently delay tail regeneration in xenopus larva, suggesting that ROS levels must be carefully regulated during regeneration (Han et al., 2014; von HAHN, 1959).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chemical inhibition of Catalase may transiently delay tail regeneration in xenopus larva.
source: Overexpression of catalase impedes heart regeneration after infarction in zebrafish, and chemical inhibition of Catalase may transiently delay tail regeneration in xenopus larva, suggesting that ROS levels must be carefully regulated during regeneration (Han et al., 2014; von HAHN, 1959).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: ROS levels must be carefully regulated during regeneration.
source: Overexpression of catalase impedes heart regeneration after infarction in zebrafish, and chemical inhibition of Catalase may transiently delay tail regeneration in xenopus larva, suggesting that ROS levels must be carefully regulated during regeneration (Han et al., 2014; von HAHN, 1959).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies showing both positive and negative effects of ROS manipulation.

claim: Fetuin-B and its paralogue Fetuin-A are highly expressed in the liver, where they are secreted into the blood plasma.
source: Fetuin-B and its paralogue Fetuin-A, are highly expressed in the liver, where they are secreted into the blood plasma, and are also expressed in the chondrocytes and muscle cells of developing limb buds in mouse, rat, and sheep (Terkelsen et al., 1998; Saunders et al., 1994; Dziegielewska et al., 1996; Denecke et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on fetuin expression.

claim: Fetuin-B and Fetuin-A are expressed in the chondrocytes and muscle cells of developing limb buds in mouse, rat, and sheep.
source: Fetuin-B and its paralogue Fetuin-A, are highly expressed in the liver, where they are secreted into the blood plasma, and are also expressed in the chondrocytes and muscle cells of developing limb buds in mouse, rat, and sheep (Terkelsen et al., 1998; Saunders et al., 1994; Dziegielewska et al., 1996; Denecke et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on fetuin expression.

claim: Mammalian Fetuins belong to the cystatin superfamily of proteins, which include many protease inhibitors.
source: Mammalian Fetuins belong to the cystatin superfamily of proteins, which include many protease inhibitors, yet these two proteins appear to have differing biochemical activities (Denecke et al., 2003; Karmilin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on fetuin protein family.

claim: Fetuin-A and Fetuin-B appear to have differing biochemical activities.
source: Mammalian Fetuins belong to the cystatin superfamily of proteins, which include many protease inhibitors, yet these two proteins appear to have differing biochemical activities (Denecke et al., 2003; Karmilin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fetuin-A is expressed in the growth plate chondrocytes of young mice and is required for proper long bone development.
source: Fetuin-A is expressed in the growth plate chondrocytes of young mice and is required for proper long bone development, and Fetuin-A knockout mice exhibit severely foreshortened femora due to growth plate deformations and displaced distal epiphyses (Seto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on Fetuin-A knockout mice.

claim: Fetuin-A knockout mice exhibit severely foreshortened femora due to growth plate deformations and displaced distal epiphyses.
source: Fetuin-A is expressed in the growth plate chondrocytes of young mice and is required for proper long bone development, and Fetuin-A knockout mice exhibit severely foreshortened femora due to growth plate deformations and displaced distal epiphyses (Seto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fetuin-B knockout mice do not display bone development defects, but instead show female infertility.
source: Fetub, knockout mice, however, do not display these defects, and instead show female infertility (Dietzel et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on Fetuin-B knockout mice.

claim: Mammalian Fetuin-B, unlike Fetuin-A, appears to function as a specific inhibitor of meprin and ovastacin metalloproteinases.
source: and mammalian Fetuin-B, unlike Fetuin-A, appears to function as a specific inhibitor of meprin and ovastacin metalloproteinases (Karmilin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on Fetuin-B function.

claim: Extracellular matrix remodeling by metalloproteinases is crucial for a variety of processes, including regeneration.
source: Extracellular matrix remodeling by metalloproteinases is crucial for a variety of processes, including regeneration.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about metalloproteinases in regeneration.

claim: Locally expressed Fetuin-B is an important regulator of regeneration in the axolotl.
source: Together, our results suggest that locally expressed Fetub is an important regulator of regeneration in the axolotl.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing negative selection of fetuin-b mutants.

claim: Both catalase and fetuin-b genes are not developmentally essential in mice.
source: Both genes for which mutant cells exhibited negative selection in this assay are not developmentally essential in mice
evidence: This is based on knowledge from cited studies on knockout mice.

claim: Transcriptional profiling indicates that a considerable portion of blastema-enriched genes are known to participate in limb development or cell survival in other organisms.
source: however, transcriptional profiling of axolotl limb blastemas across the time course of regeneration indicates that a considerable portion of blastema-enriched genes are known to participate in limb development or cell survival in other organisms (Monaghan et al., 2012; Knapp et al., 2013; Stewart et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to transcriptional profiling studies.

claim: Mosaic loss-of-function of many genes enriched in both the limb bud and limb blastema may result in a depletion of mutant cell lineages prior to limb formation.
source: We anticipate that mosaic loss-of-function of many genes enriched in both the limb bud and limb blastema may result in a depletion of mutant cell lineages prior to limb formation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential confounding effects in the assay.

claim: Mutant alleles of genes required for both limb development and regeneration may not exhibit negative selection in this assay.
source: Thus, mutant alleles of genes required for both limb development and regeneration may not exhibit negative selection in this assay.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of the assay method.

claim: The identification and validation of catalase and fetuin-b suggests that this method is particularly useful for identifying genes that are not essential for limb development but critical for proper regeneration.
source: The identification and validation of catalase and fetub in this assay suggests that this method is particularly useful for identifying genes that are not essential for limb development but critical for proper regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the successful identification of these two genes.

claim: Single-cell analyses indicate that connective-tissue-derived blastema cells transcriptionally converge to express a shared set of genes distinct from that expressed in developing limb buds.
source: Recent single-cell analyses of blastema cells across the time course of regeneration indicate that connective-tissue-derived blastema cells transcriptionally converge to express a shared set of genes distinct from that expressed in developing limb buds
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to single-cell analysis studies.

claim: At later stages of regeneration, blastema cells recapitulate transcriptional programs found in developing limbs.
source: however, at later stages of regeneration these blastema cells recapitulate transcriptional programs found in developing limbs (Gerber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to single-cell analysis studies.

claim: The genes controlling early blastema formation do not substantially overlap with those required for proper limb development.
source: These findings indicate that the genes controlling early blastema formation do not substantially overlap with those required for proper limb development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the single-cell analysis findings.

claim: The recessive short-toes allele in axolotls produces animals that develop limbs but display a progressive decline in regenerative capacity.
source: The long-characterized recessive short-toes allele in axolotls produces animals that develop limbs but display a progressive decline in regenerative capacity (Del Rio-Tsonis et al., 1992; Gassner and Tassava, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the short-toes mutant.

claim: Loss of sox2 in axolotls produces an early spinal cord regeneration defect without perturbing spinal cord development.
source: Similarly, loss of sox2 in axolotls produces an early spinal cord regeneration defect without perturbing spinal cord development (Fei et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on sox2 mutants.

claim: 16 out of 25 gRNAs used in this study produced mutant alleles in the limb of at least one animal analyzed.
source: While 16/25 gRNAs used in this study produced mutant alleles in the limb of at least one animal analyzed, we expect that in future studies injecting greater quantities of gRNA will produce more mutant alleles without confounding results.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on gRNA efficiency.

claim: Injecting greater quantities of gRNA will produce more mutant alleles without confounding results.
source: While 16/25 gRNAs used in this study produced mutant alleles in the limb of at least one animal analyzed, we expect that in future studies injecting greater quantities of gRNA will produce more mutant alleles without confounding results.
evidence: This is speculation about future experimental improvements.

claim: This method couples targeted mutagenesis and lineage tracing to identify novel regulators of regeneration.
source: Here, we provide a novel screening platform that couples targeted mutagenesis and lineage tracing to identify novel regulators of regeneration.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The development and regeneration of haploid limbs is comparable to that of diploid limbs.
source: This method relies upon the ability to generate chimeric animals that possess mutagenized haploid limbs. We find that the development and regeneration of these haploid limbs is comparable to that of diploid limbs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing haploid and diploid limbs.

claim: Catalase and fetuin-b are required for cells to participate in limb regeneration.
source: Using this approach, we find that catalase and fetuin-b are required for cells to participate in limb regeneration and for proper tail regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative selection data and tail regeneration experiments.

claim: Catalase and fetuin-b are required for proper tail regeneration.
source: Using this approach, we find that catalase and fetuin-b are required for cells to participate in limb regeneration and for proper tail regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tail regeneration experiments.

claim: This is the first example of a true in vivo haploid selection screen conducted in a complex structure of a vertebrate.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example of a true in vivo haploid selection screen conducted in a complex structure of a vertebrate.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the approach based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Chimeric embryos are generated by replacing the limb buds of GFP+ diploid embryos with corresponding tissue from mutagenized haploid donors.
source: Chimeric embryos are generated by replacing the limb buds of GFP+ diploid embryos with corresponding tissue from mutagenized haploid donors.
evidence: This describes the experimental method shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cell lineages harboring deleterious mutant alleles are predicted to be reduced in regenerated limbs.

claim: Mutagenized genes essential for regeneration will show a decrease in allele frequency or a complete loss of alleles in the regenerated limb.
